planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bluebird mountain hydrangea is more cold-hardy and reliably reblooms after a hard pruning better than many bigleaf hydrangeas.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bluebird mountain hydrangea is more cold-hardy and reliably reblooms after a hard pruning better than many bigleaf hydrangeas. Delicate, lacecap flower heads ring a center of small, fertile blue (or pink in alkaline soil) flowers with a fringe of larger, showier sterile florets, a more refined, airy bloom than the tight mophead clusters of standard bigleaf hydrangea, on a compact, well-branched shrub with narrower, more textured leaves. As a mountain hydrangea it tolerates more cold and sun than typical bigleaf hydrangeas and blooms on both old and some new wood, making it more forgiving of pruning mistakes and late spring frosts that can eliminate the year's flowers on old-wood-only cultivars. Amend soil pH to control flower color — more acidic soil produces blue tones, more alkaline soil produces pink — and mulch well to keep roots cool and moist through summer.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Mariesii doublefile viburnum develops its best horizontal, tiered branching structure with room to spread unpruned.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Mariesii doublefile viburnum develops its best horizontal, tiered branching structure with room to spread unpruned. Distinctly horizontal, layered branches are lined in spring with rows of flat, lacecap flower clusters held above the foliage on short stalks in a striking double row along each branch, giving the whole shrub a tiered, snow-covered appearance visible from a distance. One of the most architecturally striking flowering shrubs available, its strong horizontal branching habit provides four-season structural interest even without flowers, followed by red fruit that ripens to black and reliable burgundy fall color. Prune minimally and only to remove crossing or damaged branches, since heavy pruning disrupts the tiered branching pattern that is the plant's signature feature.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; European snowball bush is an old-fashioned, sterile-flowered cultivar that produces no fruit.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; European snowball bush is an old-fashioned, sterile-flowered cultivar that produces no fruit. This long-cultivated heirloom shrub bears large, perfectly round clusters of pure white flowers in late spring, opening lime-green and aging to snowy white, giving the shrub the appearance of being covered in dozens of large snowballs at peak bloom, a classic pass-along plant of old Southern and Midwestern gardens for generations. Because every flower in the cluster is sterile (unlike the fertile lacecap flowers of the wild species), it produces no berries, trading wildlife food value for a much showier, fuller flower display. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning removes the following year's flowers; watch for aphids, which favor the tender new growth of this species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Natchez mock orange was bred in the South for good heat and humidity tolerance and performs reliably in Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Natchez mock orange was bred in the South for good heat and humidity tolerance and performs reliably in Gulf South gardens. Large, pure white, four-petaled flowers smother the arching branches in late spring, filling the garden with an intense, sweet orange-blossom fragrance that gives mock orange its common name, on a vigorous, upright shrub bred at Louisiana State University specifically for improved performance in hot, humid southern climates. Its strong Southern breeding heritage makes it a more reliable performer in Gulf Coast gardens than many older mock orange selections developed for cooler, drier climates, retaining good foliage quality through summer heat. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, since it blooms on old wood and later pruning sacrifices the next season's fragrant display.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Prince weigela is valued for holding its red flower color without fading in heat better than many older red weigela cultivars.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Prince weigela is valued for holding its red flower color without fading in heat better than many older red weigela cultivars. Masses of vivid, true-red, trumpet-shaped flowers smother the arching branches in late spring, with a lighter rebloom often following in summer, on a vigorous, cold-hardy shrub with clean green foliage that provides a dependable backbone of bright color for a mixed shrub border. Its non-fading red flower color and strong cold tolerance made it a standard, widely planted weigela cultivar for decades, valued by gardeners for its reliability over showier but less hardy newer introductions. Prune immediately after the main spring flush to shape and encourage rebloom, since it flowers primarily on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; virginal mock orange is a classic, widely grown hybrid group prized for heavily double, intensely fragrant flowers.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; virginal mock orange is a classic, widely grown hybrid group prized for heavily double, intensely fragrant flowers. Large, semi-double to fully double, pure white flowers cover the upright, somewhat leggy branches in late spring, carrying an intense, sweet orange-blossom fragrance that made this old hybrid group a mainstay of cottage and heritage gardens since the early twentieth century. Less refined in habit than some newer compact mock orange cultivars, it is grown chiefly for the strength of its fragrance and flower fullness, best sited toward the back of a border or near a window or path where the scent can be appreciated during its bloom period. Prune immediately after flowering, removing some of the oldest canes each year at the base to keep the naturally leggy shrub renewed and full at the bottom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Cloud beautybush flowers most heavily in full sun and tolerates poor soil and drought once established.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Pink Cloud beautybush flowers most heavily in full sun and tolerates poor soil and drought once established. In late spring the entire arching, fountain-shaped shrub disappears beneath a dense, week-long cloud of small, bell-shaped, soft pink flowers with a yellow throat, a bloom so heavy it can obscure the foliage entirely, followed by bristly, bronze-pink seed capsules that add subtle texture into fall. Selected for its especially profuse, richly colored bloom compared to the species, it is an easy, tough, low-maintenance shrub once established, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil with minimal care, and its peeling, tan-brown bark provides winter interest after the leaves drop. Prune immediately after flowering to shape, removing some of the oldest stems at ground level each year to keep the shrub renewed and full from the base.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Longwood Blue bluebeard is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Longwood Blue bluebeard is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring. Aromatic, silvery-green foliage sets off dense clusters of vivid, true-blue, fringed flowers that wreathe the upper stems from late summer into fall, a bloom period that provides valuable late-season nectar for bees and butterflies when many other shrubs have finished flowering. Introduced by Longwood Gardens and prized for its especially rich, saturated blue flower color compared to older caryopteris cultivars, it is a compact, easy-care choice for the front or middle of a sunny border, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established. Cut the whole plant back to a few inches from the ground in late winter, since it flowers on new wood and benefits from hard annual pruning to stay compact and floriferous.
